+# `mormot.net.tunnel` — End-to-End Tunnel Security and Deployment Guidance
+
+**Scope:** mORMot2 local TCP forwarding through `ITunnelTransmit`, including `TTunnelLocalServer`, `TTunnelLocalClient`, the relay interfaces, the `tlmVersion2` handshake, and authenticated encrypted TCP payloads. The principal example is administrator-to-agent remote assistance carrying VNC/RFB through a relay.
+
+**Implementation:** [`src/net/mormot.net.tunnel.pas`](../../src/net/mormot.net.tunnel.pas).  
+**Cryptographic dependencies:** [`mormot.crypt.ecc256r1.pas`](../../src/crypt/mormot.crypt.ecc256r1.pas), [`mormot.crypt.core.pas`](../../src/crypt/mormot.crypt.core.pas), and `ICryptCert` in [`mormot.crypt.secure.pas`](../../src/crypt/mormot.crypt.secure.pas).  
+**Related tests:** [`test/test.net.proto.pas`](../../test/test.net.proto.pas) (`TNetworkProtocols.Tunnel`, `TunnelTest`, `TunnelRelay`, `TunnelDeferred`) and [`test/test.core.ecc.pas`](../../test/test.core.ecc.pas).
+
+**Review basis:** Inspection of the current trunk implementation, cryptographic construction, protocol invariants, threat boundaries, and existing tests. This is a source-level engineering security review: it is **not** a formal cryptographic proof, external certification, fuzzing report, or assertion that the complete application has been penetration-tested.
+
+> **Executive assessment.** `tlmVersion2` provides a compact end-to-end TCP tunnel with optional P-256 ECDHE, role-separated AES-128-GCM traffic keys, 128-bit GCM authentication tags, per-frame evolving nonces, and optional endpoint certificate signatures. A sufficiently unpredictable, confidential `AppSecret` provides an alternative shared-secret authenticator for the fixed handshake, without certificates. The relay routes opaque traffic and does not need the established ECDHE traffic keys.
+>
+> **Essential condition.** Encryption and authentication are separate properties. Against an **active, malicious relay**, use `[toEcdhe]` **and** authenticate the endpoint with a separately trusted `VerifyCert` or a **strong, independently provisioned `AppSecret`**. ECDHE with an empty/known secret and no certificate can be intercepted by an active man-in-the-middle. The application remains responsible for authorization, endpoint selection, user consent, and credential provisioning.
+
+## 1. Security goals and trust boundaries
+
+A representative topology is:
+
+```text
+Administrator console                   Relay / transport                    End-user agent
+VNC viewer --local TCP-- TTunnelLocalServer ===== TunnelSend frames ===== TTunnelLocalClient --local TCP-- VNC server
+                         <-------------- P-256 ECDHE + AES-128-GCM -------------->
+                            Endpoint authentication occurs at each endpoint
+```
+
+The endpoint cryptographic server/client roles can be reversed, and the relay transport need not be WebSockets. See section 3 for the distinction between administrator console, end-user agent, SOA service endpoints, and local TCP processes. `TTunnelLocal` protects the bytes carried between the two local forwarding endpoints; it does not provide access control for the local application protocol itself.
+
+| Property | Intended protection | Trust boundary |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| TCP payload confidentiality | AES-128-GCM when `toEcdhe` or `toEncrypt` is enabled | Requires an authenticated handshake against an active attacker |
+| TCP payload integrity | 128-bit GCM tag checked before writing plaintext to the local socket | A relay may still drop, delay, reorder, or terminate frames |
+| Endpoint authentication | Trusted peer certificate signature, and/or proof of a strong shared `AppSecret` | Trust anchors/secrets must be provisioned by the application |
+| Forward secrecy | Fresh P-256 ECDHE key material for each tunnel | Does not apply to static `SpecificKey` reuse or PSK-only `toEncrypt` |
+| Session association | Handshake session value and GCM additional authen
... [truncated, 52876 more chars]

+# Windows SChannel TLS and Server mTLS — Design, Security Rationale, and Implementation Review
+
+**Scope:** Native Windows SChannel TLS client and HTTPS/TLS server in mORMot 2, with particular attention to mutual TLS (mTLS), certificate trust, callbacks, connection state, and the OpenSSL compatibility contract.  
+**Source snapshot:** mORMot 2 **2.4.17601**, [`c3e08fe860a464af36a839c7b5c69a76cae0cc71`](https://github.com/synopse/mORMot2/tree/c3e08fe860a464af36a839c7b5c69a76cae0cc71) (13 October 2026, `master` at review time).  
+**Primary implementation:** [`mormot.net.sock.windows.inc`](../../src/net/mormot.net.sock.windows.inc) ([reviewed revision](https://github.com/synopse/mORMot2/blob/c3e08fe860a464af36a839c7b5c69a76cae0cc71/src/net/mormot.net.sock.windows.inc)).  
+**API and integration:** [`mormot.net.sock.pas`](../../src/net/mormot.net.sock.pas), [`mormot.net.server.pas`](../../src/net/mormot.net.server.pas), and [`mormot.lib.sspi.pas`](../../src/lib/mormot.lib.sspi.pas).  
+**OpenSSL comparison:** [`mormot.lib.openssl11.pas`](../../src/lib/mormot.lib.openssl11.pas).  
+**Tests:** [`test.net.proto.pas`](../../test/test.net.proto.pas), `TNetworkProtocols._SChannel` (Windows with `USE_OPENSSL`).  
+**Review method:** Static inspection of the pinned implementation, its API and test source, plus relevant Microsoft API contracts. **No Windows build or integration test was executed in this review.**
+
+> **Engineering conclusion.** The native SChannel backend deliberately provides a **dependency-light Windows TLS transport** with normal operating-system server-certificate validation on the client and optional **server-side client-certificate authentication**. For mTLS, the implementation requests a certificate through SSPI, obtains the remote certificate, builds and evaluates a client-authentication chain with CryptoAPI, and rejects a missing or invalid certificate **unless an application-installed per-certificate callback explicitly overrides the validation result**. Explicit trust anchors are isolated in a private chain engine; TLS and certificate resources have well-defined ownership across accepted connections.
+>
+> The intended default is straightforward: **use ordinary one-way TLS unless client identity authentication is required; for mTLS, enable `ClientCertificateAuthentication`, configure the appropriate trusted CA set, and leave validation callbacks unset unless they enforce a carefully designed additional policy.** The callback override, offline-revocation tolerance, Windows-specific trust-anchor behavior, and currently absent SChannel client-certificate configuration are **real boundaries**, not properties that documentation should hide. This is an implementation-oriented security review, **not a claim of formal certification or an audit of Microsoft's TLS stack**.
+
+## 1. Goals, boundaries, and threat model
+
+### 1.1 Responsibilities and design intent
+
+| Component | Responsibility | Security-relevant code/API |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `TNetTlsContext`, `INetTls` | Shared TLS configuration and stable caller/backend contract | `AfterConnection`, `AfterBind`, `AfterAccept`, `ResetNetTlsContext` |
+| `TSChannelNetTls` | One connection's SSPI context, handshake, encrypted records, post-handshake processing, output fields | `CredInit`, `HandshakeLoop`, `Receive`, `Send`, `GetRawTls` |
+| `TSChannelServerContext` | Shared inbound credential, server certificate, private client trust, mTLS chain verification | `LoadCertificate`, `LoadClientTrust`, `ValidateClientCertificate` |
+| Windows SSPI / SChannel | TLS negotiation, cryptographic traffic protection, remote certificate retrieval | `AcquireCredentialsHandleW`, `InitializeSecurityContextW`, `AcceptSecurityContext`, `QueryContextAttributesW` |
+| Windows CryptoAPI / certificate wrappers | Certificate decoding, chain construction, chain policy, trust stores, context ownership | `CertGetCertificateChain`, `CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy`, `TWin

+# `mormot.crypt.rsa` — RSA Design, Security Rationale, and Implementation Review
+
+**Scope:** mORMot2 native RSA engine for Delphi and Free Pascal; cryptographic algorithms, implementation invariants, and production usage.  
+**Source snapshot:** mORMot2 **2.4.17599**, [`efdf73f3e20f`](https://github.com/synopse/mORMot2/tree/efdf73f3e20fe620ee0ce03f8bd2a0bdcaf49527) (13 October 2026).  
+**Implementation:** [`src/crypt/mormot.crypt.rsa.pas`](../../src/crypt/mormot.crypt.rsa.pas) ([reviewed source](https://github.com/synopse/mORMot2/blob/efdf73f3e20fe620ee0ce03f8bd2a0bdcaf49527/src/crypt/mormot.crypt.rsa.pas)).  
+**Supporting code and tests:** [`mormot.crypt.core.pas`](../../src/crypt/mormot.crypt.core.pas), [`test.core.crypt.pas`](../../test/test.core.crypt.pas).  
+**Companion CSPRNG design:** [`TAesPrng.md`](TAesPrng.md).
+
+> **Engineering conclusion.** The built-in RSA engine uses well-established number theory, probabilistic primality testing, standards-based PKCS#1 encodings, and a CSPRNG-backed generation path. Its defaults are intended to be useful **without application-specific tuning**: RSA-2048 generation, exponent 65537, appropriate primality-test rounds, fresh cryptographic randomness, fixed-width signatures, and high-level signature self-verification. The optimized arithmetic and cross-platform Pascal/assembly implementations support mORMot's priorities: **safe and unsurprising defaults, portability, and speed**.
+>
+> This document records how those design choices work, the applicable portions of FIPS 186-5 and RFC 8017, source inspection and independent algorithm checks, and the separate responsibilities of callers using legacy encryption formats or special-purpose deployment policies. It is an engineering security review, not a replacement for production testing.
+
+## 1. Scope, goals, and trust boundaries
+
+`mormot.crypt.rsa` supplies a native Pascal RSA engine for Delphi and Free Pascal. Its responsibilities include:
+
+| Component | Responsibility | Security-relevant interface |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| `TBigInt` | Non-negative multiprecision integers, arithmetic, primality tests, candidate generation | `IsPrime`, `FillPrime`, `PrimeAllowedFor65537`, `Release` |
+| `TRsaContext` | BigInt ownership and free list, cached moduli, Barrett reduction, exponentiation | `Allocate`, `Reduce`, `ModPower`, `WipeReleased` |
+| `TRsa` | RSA key pairs, CRT operations, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5, hybrid envelope | `GenerateNew`, `CheckPrivateKey`, `Sign`, `Verify`, `Seal`, `Open` |
+| `TRsaPss` | RSASSA-PSS encoding, signing, verification | `Sign`, `Verify` |
+| `TRsaPrimeWorker` | Independent concurrent generation of one RSA prime | `Execute`, `Destroy` |
+| Crypto catalog adapters | Framework integration and algorithm selection | `RS256`/`RS384`/`RS512`, `PS256`/`PS384`/`PS512` and internal aliases |
+
+The audit assumes a trusted host process, sufficiently unpredictable operating-system entropy, correct compiler/runtime and platform integer semantics, and protected private-key storage. Inputs such as ciphertexts, public keys, signatures, and externally supplied DER/PEM/JWK material may be untrusted. Physical compromise, malicious native code running in the process, and active control of the entropy source are outside the promised protections.
+
+`RS256-int` and `PS256-int` expose this engine even if the default cryptographic catalog is configured to use OpenSSL. Testing the intended backend is essential.
+
+### 1.1 What the default contract provides
+
+- **Mathematical correctness:** BigInt arithmetic, CRT reconstruction, probable-prime generation, modular inverses, and consistent RSA key parameters.
+- **Standards-oriented encodings:** RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and RSASSA-PSS implementations following RFC 8017; deterministic v1.5 encodings are compared exactly.
+- **Responsible cryptographic randomness:** `FillRandomTrusted()` supplies the initial prime-candidate seed from suitable external/CSPRN
